\chapter{Seasons}
\label{ch:hi-seasons}
\hlchaptermodality{14}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name all six traditional Indian seasons in Hindi, including the one the four-season frame has no word for.}

Say all six \hi{ऋतु} in order and point to \hi{वर्षा}, the monsoon season no Western four-season label maps onto.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\hi{वसंत} \hi{ग्रीष्म} \hi{वर्षा} \hi{शरद्} \hi{हेमंत} \hi{शिशिर}]{\hi{वसंत}, \hi{ग्रीष्म}, \hi{वर्षा}, \hi{शरद्}, \hi{हेमंत}, \hi{शिशिर} — six seasons, not four}

\label{lesson:HI-C14-ritu}



\begin{quote}
European languages generally split the year into \textbf{four} seasons. Hindi's own tradition doesn't — it recognizes \textbf{six}, and this isn't extra vocabulary bolted onto a four-season frame. It's a genuinely different way of dividing the year.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The six \hi{ऋतु} (ṛtu, \textquotedblleft{}seasons\textquotedblright{})}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Hindi} & \textbf{rough Western match} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\hi{वसंत}} (\emph{vasant}) & spring \\
\textbf{\hi{ग्रीष्म}} (\emph{grīṣma}) & summer \\
\textbf{\hi{वर्षा}} (\emph{varṣā}) & \textbf{monsoon/rains} — no Western equivalent \\
\textbf{\hi{शरद्}} (\emph{śarad}) & autumn \\
\textbf{\hi{हेमंत}} (\emph{hemant}) & pre-winter/late autumn \\
\textbf{\hi{शिशिर}} (\emph{śiśir}) & deep winter \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

This six-season calendar, \textbf{\hi{ऋतु}} (\emph{ṛtu}), is rooted in classical Sanskrit tradition and Indian astronomy/astrology, and it maps onto the actual climate of much of the Indian subcontinent far better than a four-season frame does: the \textbf{monsoon} (\emph{varṣā}) is a real, distinct, and hugely important season there — not a subdivision of \textquotedblleft{}summer\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}autumn,\textquotedblright{} but its own season with no clean Western counterpart. And the cold season splits into \textbf{two} stages, \emph{hemant} (the onset) and \emph{śiśir} (deep winter), rather than being lumped into one \textquotedblleft{}winter.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest: don't force the four-season frame onto this}
It would be a mistake to just match these six words one-to-one against Spanish's four or French's four the way earlier lessons matched \emph{tala} to \emph{talai}. The \textbf{structure itself is different} — six real seasons, not four plus two extras. Everyday spoken Hindi \emph{does} also use looser, more casual four-part talk about seasons (borrowing straightforwardly from the idea of \textquotedblleft{}summer,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}winter,\textquotedblright{} etc.), but the traditional, classical \hi{ऋतु} system is genuinely six-fold, and it's worth learning as its own thing rather than squeezed into someone else's frame.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all six — \textquotedblleft{}vasant, grīṣma, varṣā, śarad, hemant, śiśir\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one with no Western match — \textquotedblleft{}varṣā,\textquotedblright{} the monsoon
  \item the honest point — six seasons is a different STRUCTURE, not extra vocabulary
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many seasons does Hindi's traditional \hi{ऋतु} calendar recognize? (\textbf{Six}, not four.) Which season has no clean Western equivalent, and why? (\textbf{\hi{वर्षा}} \emph{varṣā}, the \textbf{monsoon} — a real, distinct season central to the subcontinent's climate.) Is this just extra vocabulary added to a four-season frame? (\textbf{No} — it's a genuinely different structural division of the year.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[candrabindu]{\hi{◌ँ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:HI-S118-sign-candrabindu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \hi{च} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{◌ँ}}
\textbf{\hi{◌ँ}} — \emph{a nasal, ridden on the syllable before it}.

It is a \textbf{nasal vowel} mark — the vowel itself is spoken through the nose, rather than a nasal consonant being added after it.

You already say these, and every one of them has \hi{◌ँ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{चलता} \hi{हूँ}} — I'll be off (lit. \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{}), gendered
  \item \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ}} — I speak Hindi (gendered)
  \item \textbf{\hi{बोलता} \hi{हूँ}, \hi{बोलती} \hi{हूँ}, \hi{बोलते} \hi{हैं}} — the present-habitual template — stem + -tā/-tī/-te + honā
  \item \textbf{\hi{पाँच}} \emph{pāṁch} — Sanskrit's nasal consonant survives inside the Hindi vowel
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{◌ँ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \hi{◌ँ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \hi{◌ँ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{◌ँ} three times, humming the nasal at the end of the syllable as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \hi{◌ँ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \hi{◌ँ}? What does it add to the syllable before it? (\textbf{A nasal.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
